neet_che_u17_t03_1.working: With bromine water, phenol undergoes trisubstitution because the -OH (and phenoxide) group strongly activates the ring. The product is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which forms as a white precipitate.

neet_che_u17_t03_2.working: o-Nitrophenol has intramolecular H-bonding, so it does not associate with other molecules and is steam volatile. p-Nitrophenol has intermolecular H-bonding, so it is less volatile. The ortho isomer therefore distils over.

neet_che_u17_t03_3.working: Sulphonation is reversible. At higher temperature (about 373 K) the thermodynamically more stable para product, p-phenolsulphonic acid, is the major product.

neet_che_u17_t03_4.working: A: Br2 in CS2 at low temperature gives mainly p-bromophenol (II). B: bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol (III). C: dilute HNO3 at 298 K gives a mixture of o- and p-nitrophenol (IV). D: conc. HNO3 gives picric acid (I).

neet_che_u17_t03_5.working: A is true: -OH activates the ring and directs ortho/para by +R. B is false: phenol is reactive enough that no Lewis acid is needed. C is true: phenoxide forms in water and is more activating, giving tribromination. D is true: per NCERT, sulphonation then nitration gives a better yield because direct nitration causes oxidation. E is false: near room temperature the ortho isomer is the main product. So A, C and D are correct.
